summary.text: Galaxy morphological classification is how astronomers divide galaxies into groups based on their visual appearance, shape, structure and distribution of light.
The most famous scheme is the Hubble sequence, devised by Edwin Hubble, which covers ellipticals, spirals, barred spirals, lenticulars and irregulars.
Gérard de Vaucouleurs extended it in 1959 to cover rings and lenses, and today classification is largely done with computational methods.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting galaxies by looks
paragraphs.text: Galaxy classification sorts galaxies into groups by how they look: their shape, their structure and the way their light is spread out. Astronomers use several schemes for this. The best known is the Hubble sequence, created by Edwin Hubble and later extended by Gérard de Vaucouleurs and Allan Sandage. It is still the most widely used system, by professional researchers and amateurs alike, although much of the sorting today is done with computer methods.

paragraphs.heading: The main classes
paragraphs.text: Spiral galaxies, given the symbol S, have a flat disk in which stars trace a spiral, usually with two arms, plus a central crowd of stars called the bulge. That bulge looks much like an elliptical galaxy. About half of all spirals also show a bar-like structure running out from the bulge, and these barred spirals get the symbol SB. Lenticular galaxies, written S0, also have a bright bulge inside a disk, but the disk shows no spiral and makes hardly any new stars. Irregular galaxies have no obvious regular structure, neither disk-like nor egg-shaped.

paragraphs.heading: The tuning fork
paragraphs.text: The Hubble sequence is often drawn as a fork with two prongs. Ellipticals sit on the left, growing more stretched as you move to the right. Barred and unbarred spirals form the two parallel prongs on the right, and lenticulars sit where the prongs meet the handle. Even so, in June 2019 volunteers working through Galaxy Zoo reported that the usual scheme may need rethinking, especially in how it links spiral arms to a galaxy's central nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: Adding rings and lenses
paragraphs.text: In 1959 Gérard de Vaucouleurs described a widely used extension of Hubble's scheme. He argued that Hubble's two measures for spirals, how tightly the arms wind and whether there is a bar, missed much of the range of shapes actually seen. In particular, he held that rings and lenses are important parts of spiral galaxies. His labels are joined in a fixed order, so a weakly barred spiral with loosely wound arms and a ring is written SAB(r)c. Drawn out, his system is a three-dimensional tuning fork, with spiralness, barredness and ringedness along its three axes.

paragraphs.heading: Putting numbers on shape
paragraphs.text: De Vaucouleurs also gave each class a number, the Hubble stage T, which runs from −6 to +10. Negative values mark early types, the ellipticals and lenticulars, and positive values mark late types, the spirals and irregulars. As a rough rule, a lower T means more of a galaxy's stellar mass sits in its bulge rather than its disk. For nearby galaxies the link is roughly M_B/M_T=(10−T)²/256, where M_B/M_T is the ratio of bulge stellar mass to total stellar mass. Numbers like these let astronomers study galaxy shapes in a more measured way.

paragraphs.heading: Other ways to classify
paragraphs.text: Other schemes exist too. The Yerkes scheme, made by the American astronomer William Wilson Morgan, uses the spectra of a galaxy's stars, its real and apparent shape, and how concentrated it is toward the center; under it the Andromeda Galaxy is kS5. In 1998 Sidney van den Bergh published a book probing weak points in the Hubble sequence. Number-based tools followed: in 2003 Christopher Conselice formalized the CAS parameters, and in 2004 Jennifer Lotz found that the Gini coefficient, used with a measure called M₂₀ and the CAS parameters, could tell normal galaxies apart from mergers.
